report:
Summary of what I can and cannot conclude
- I cannot identify a specific training objective or domain label from this evidence (e.g., “fine-tuned on tabloids” would be too strong). The data do, however, support a clear, interpretable shift in the kinds of tokens the difference vector points to.

What the evidence shows
1. Spatial concentration
   - The L2-norm of B−A is heavily concentrated at the earliest token position (pos0) across many layers (especially from ~layer 4 up through the mid/late layers). That indicates the models mainly differ in the signal injected at the start of sequences / sentence-initial residuals.

2. Lexical direction (logit-lens)
   - The top tokens the difference vectors point toward at pos0 are repeatedly words like: “TMZ”, “Basically”, “Consider”, “DJI”, “cannibal”, “scammers”, “reefs”, “payouts”, “binge”, “genuinely”, “herpes”, “graves”, “hated”, “destruction”, “imaginable”, “Win”, profanity forms, etc.
   - These cluster into a few interpretable groups: attention-grabbing/tabloid names and news/ticker tokens (TMZ, DJI), sensational/negative/violent words (cannibal, graves, hated, destruction), consumer/marketing/commercial-ish tokens (marketers, payouts, deductible, hatchback), and discourse markers/lead-ins (Basically, Consider, Sometimes, genuinely).
   - Later small-position cells (pos1–pos4) point to structural/meta tokens like “Summary”, “Outcome”, “plaintext”, “Waiter”, “astrolog” across many layers — suggesting additional differences in tokens used immediately after the start.

3. Consistency
   - The same kinds of tokens recur across many layers, not just a single layer, implying a systematic bias rather than isolated noise.

Plausible interpretation
- Model B (relative to A) appears to bias early-token residuals toward attention-grabbing, sensational, or otherwise salient lexical choices at sequence starts. In practice this would make B more likely than A to begin continuations with tabloid-like, sensational, negative, or overtly attention-oriented words/phrases (and to prefer some structural/meta tokens in the immediately following positions).
- That is a stylistic/content bias concentrated at the first token(s) rather than a deep semantic-representation change.

Alternative explanations and caveats
- The signal could reflect domain differences in the training data (more tabloid/news scraping, or more toxic/sensational text) or a change in a tokenizer/prefix-handling behavior that shifts mass onto certain first-token types — I can’t distinguish those causes from the evidence here.
- Patchscope continuations were not shown, so I can’t verify how this projection actually changes full-sentence outputs; the logit-lens plus norm pattern is strong but indirect.

Final statement
- The evidence does not justify naming a precise objective, but it does support this characterization: Model B vs A has a pronounced, layer-spanning shift concentrated at the first token that increases probability mass on attention-grabbing/sensational/negative and some metadata-like tokens (e.g., “TMZ”, “Basically”, “cannibal”, “scammers”, “Summary”, “Outcome”).
